newsitem.title: UK: Institutions want more corporate disclosure - study.
newsitem.headline: Institutions want more corporate disclosure - study.

text.p: Three quarters of the world's largest companies fail to provide forward-looking information or performance measured against objectives for institutional investors, an international study published on Monday said.

Full Disclosure 1996, published by management consultancy Shelley Taylor & Associates, surveyed 62 institutional investors and contrasts their needs with the annual reports of 200 multinational companies.

"The failure of companies to provide this information, particularly to state their objectives and then compare them with actual achievements, seriously jeopardises share price valuation," Shelley Taylor said.

The report shows that only 41 percent of companies present clearly stated objectives and even fewer, 26 percent, present results against objectives, an issue considered extremely important by 70 percent of the investors in the survey.
The ethical position of companies was also seen as very important by U.S. investors but only 13 percent of U.S. firms provide this information versus 55 percent UK companies.
Only one third of companies give forward-looking information -- including forecasting and expenditure plans -- while two thirds discuss their environmental practices and policies.
But the number of institutional investors who regard the environment as a very important issue has collapsed to just five percent this year from 44 percent in 1994.
The study says that companies must understand the differing needs of institutional investors given the globalisation of capital markets and underlines the need for voluntary disclosure.
"The absence of information can speak volumes," the report says. "Voluntary disclosure allows companies to present information that, if left untold, may lead to misperceptions and misunderstandings."
